lede: Where the sources speak about the same thing, their voices stand side by side.

pairs.frage: What did it cost to send a crate of vegetables from Williston in 1898, and did it matter which railroad one chose?
pairs.note: Both tables give Williston the same rates: ten cents a crate of vegetables and sixteen a box of oranges, on the Plant System to High Springs and on the Florida Central & Peninsular to Jacksonville, Fernandina, Yulee or Baldwin, each “for beyond”. The state commission set them by the mile; the charge onward to the northern markets was not in its power.

pairs.frage: How did the gazetteers describe Williston before and after the railroads?
pairs.note: In 1886 Archer is the shipping point and Williston has one general store; in 1907 Williston is an incorporated town on two railroads, with a bank, two hotels and a newspaper, and “one of the greatest cucumber districts in the state”. Both entries were supplied for commercial directories and read like advertisements; the populations they give, 100 and 200, are claims, not counts.

pairs.frage: How did the officials and the lessee describe the convict camps in Levy County?
pairs.note: The department wrote in 1895 that the camps were “in charge of sober, reliable and humane men”, and its chaplain found Bailey's camp in Levy County good in every respect. Two years later Bailey himself reported twenty-one dead in 1895 and nineteen in 1896, three of them killed while escaping or being recaptured, and children under thirteen among those sent to him. All three voices are those of the state and the lessee; the prisoners are not heard.

pairs.frage: Where did the hard rock go, and what happened when it could not?
pairs.note: In 1893 a trade correspondent found that only an eighth or a seventh of Florida's phosphate stayed at home, and called it a fact that called “for serious thought”. In 1914 the war in Europe proved him right: the hard rock fields, which sold almost nothing at home, lost most of their trade within a year.

pairs.frage: How much work did the cucumbers take, and whose?
pairs.note: The railroad told prospective settlers in 1914 that cucumbers required “a small amount of labor and little expense”. The agricultural college's survey of the 1923 season found labour the largest single expense of the farms around Williston, a third of the total, paid to day labourers, contract pickers and sharecroppers. Neither source says who these workers were.

pairs.frage: How many carloads of cucumbers left Williston in a day?
pairs.note: Nine in one day by hearsay in 1907; twenty-two a day at the height of the 1910 season; thirteen to twenty a day in the peak week of 1919, by the produce trade's count. The “seventy-five carloads a day” of recent accounts has no source of the time.

pairs.frage: How did the count of the dead change in the reports of the time?
pairs.note: On 5 January five dead were “known” and many more “believed”. On 8 January the Associated Press counted seven, two white and five Black. In February the grand jury reports gave eight, two white and six Black, and the Miami report tied a ninth killing, the lynching of Abe Wilson near Newberry, to the same events. Only the white dead were named from the first day. The figure of eight remained the official one; later accounts dispute it.

pairs.frage: How was the destruction of Rosewood judged in 1923?
pairs.note: A Florida editor found that Levy County's people deserved “no censure” and were “not actually ashamed”; a newspaper in Madras, reprinted by the NAACP, saw a “great blot on American civilization” and those responsible “let go unpunished”. The grand jury in between returned no indictment.

pairs.frage: Whom do the reports name, and whom not?
pairs.note: In 1904 the paper names the victim of the shooting, the lynched man and the two Black men who caught him, but no one in the mob. In 1923 it names the white dead and wounded with their families on the first day, and the first Black victim, James Carrier, only when describing his killing; his killers are “several white men”. The only person ever named as a leader of the mob was named by the NAACP's magazine, not by any court.
